Mermaid source

Preferred syntax: block. Fixed categorical cells; membership appears in comments.

Framing

What a corpus needs to move onto the Protocol's capabilities at scale and keep designing fast. First the reach of a body and a rules file: shipped recipes called as functions, recipes that answer as rules files, rules and parameter files watched, outside registers checked by pattern, help on every verb and one verb that writes every projection root. Then keys that survive rewording, for example steps and for Model terms, and the test lines that cite a pinned declaration. Then reading material that fits a budget in parts. Last, the order a person makes the waiting statements in, and the kit that shows a corpus what it could adopt next. Each Spec is followed by the examples that verify it.

spec:consumers.agent-surface.evaluation-sink

The evaluation sink runs one body and prints its return

spec:consumers.agent-surface.evaluation-sinkUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 7 design entries · 3 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

Without a way to call a shipped recipe, a body that needs its answer pastes the recipe's file into its own text, and a rules file keeps its own copy of the recipe's code. The recipes binding lets a body call a shipped recipe by its catalog number over the graph it already holds, so the answer is the recipe's own and nothing derives twice. A recipe call is a binding, never a reader verb: the catalog stays the one owner of the bodies, and the reader gains no query vocabulary. The package exports the same evaluator, so a script that holds a graph runs a body, or a shipped recipe through that body, without deriving the graph again.

Intent
problem
How sdp q takes a body, prints its answer and refuses is stated only in the CLI help and the reading skill, so a caller and a script that runs a recipe learn the contract by trial.
outcome
State how the evaluation sink takes a body, renders its return and refuses, so every caller relies on one contract.
Behavior
rule line 19 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:19
sdp q takes one positional JavaScript async-function body, which takes precedence over stdin; with no positional body it reads non-terminal stdin, and absent, unreadable or empty input refuses with exit 1 before evaluation.
rule line 20 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:20
The sink supplies g, graph, report and params, permits await and prints the returned value using bounded util.inspect by default or JSON.stringify with --json; it does not suppress console output, so machine-consumed bodies must avoid it.
rule line 21 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:21
A body that returns undefined prints no answer, reports on stderr that return is the output contract and exits 0; a --json result with no JSON form or one that cannot be serialized refuses with exit 1 and no rendered answer.
rule line 22 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:22
An extraction error prevents evaluation, renders the extraction findings and exits 1; validation findings are supplied as report and do not gate evaluation. A compilation, evaluation or rendering failure exits 1 and reports its error on stderr.
rule line 23 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:23
A body that fails to parse is reported with the line and column of the error in the body the caller wrote.
rule.fifthBinding line 24 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:24
The sink supplies a fifth binding, recipes, beside g, graph, report and params, and every body it, the rules runner or the exported evaluator runs receives it, a recipe called through it included.

rule.recipeCall line 25 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:25
A body calls a shipped recipe as a function of its catalog number and one parameters object; the call runs the recipe's body over the caller's own g, graph and report, with no second derivation and no copy, and resolves to the recipe's answer unchanged, { unknownParams, accepts } and { diagnostics } included.

spec:consumers.agent-surface.evaluation-sink.exported-evaluator · enabled, spec:consumers.agent-surface.evaluation-sink.recipe-call · enabled

rule.callRefusals line 26 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.sdp.md:26
A call names a recipe the catalog holds and passes one plain object or nothing; any other number or parameters reject the call with a message naming the recipe, and a recipe that throws rejects the call with its error, so a mistaken call fails loudly instead of answering for a sample.

sdp q, the rules runner and the exported evaluator compile and run a body one way: the same compilation, the same parse error with its line and column, worded by each surface in its own pinned text, and the same five bindings.

specs/consumers/agent-surface.evaluation-sink.exported-evaluator.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Execute a recipe call with a parameter through evaluateBody over a graph the script derived once, and compare its answer with the recipe's shipped file evaluated over the same graph.
assumptions
  • The world writes the probe corpus of the recipe-call example and derives its graph once with the package's extract. It awaits evaluateBody with the body return recipes(26, { severity: "warning" }); and that graph, then awaits evaluateBody with the text of dist/recipes/26-dependency-cycles.js, the same graph and the parameters { severity: "warning" }, and compares the two answers. Neither call derives the graph.
Behavior

Examples

Given a probe corpus in which two Specs depend on each other through dependsOn
Given a body that calls {call: "recipe 26 with the severity warning"}
When the body runs {entrance: "through the exported evaluator over a graph derived once"}
Then the call {outcome: "resolves"}
Then the answer equals the shipped recipe file's own answer over the same graph and parameters: {sameAnswer: true}

5. Corpus-authored rules run on the one validation path

spec:validation.corpus-rules

Corpus-authored rules run on the one validation path

spec:validation.corpus-rulesUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:corpus-checks-v1, pack:design-management-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 11 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/validation/corpus-rules.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

The original design let a team add its own rules beside the built-in validators, each with an id, a severity and the whole graph query API, run in the same pass and reported in the same output (docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md §6.5). The Protocol has two check families, conformance and honesty, and every validator belongs to one of them. The architectural annotation decision sends a corpus's own rules to the corpus's own gate.

The first adopter's gate runs sdp validate and parses its summary line, then checks its own context isolation, entry addresses, dependency cycles, question keys, prose mentions, cited laws and Pack pages. It also parses carrier frontmatter to read kind, readiness and relations, a second read model that a graph-based corpus-rule runner would remove.

A rules file holds the body sdp q evaluates, so a rule tried through sdp q runs unchanged under sdp validate, and a catalog recipe whose answer carries findings, such as the architecture walk, is a rules file as shipped. A rules file that needs a shipped recipe's answer calls it through recipes and keeps no copy of its code. The runner reads only the answer's findings, so the recipe keeps the rest of its answer for a reader. Corpus findings print after the Protocol's and are tallied on a line of their own, so a gate that reads the Protocol's summary line reads it unchanged; any error, the Protocol's or the corpus's, exits 1, and the two lines say which. Each rules file receives its own copy of what it reads, so a careless rule cannot change another rule's input and the order of the files changes only the order of the output. Its parameters are its own too: a catalog recipe answers a parameter name it does not take with that name and no findings, so parameters shared by every file would fail the walk on the names another file reads.

Intent
problem
A corpus with rules of its own checks them off the one validation path, reading the carriers a second way and reporting in a form no Protocol surface reads.
outcome
Let a corpus author its own graph rules and have their findings join the one validation report, so no corpus re-parses its carriers to check itself.
Behavior

Design view

Requirement drawing

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.architectural-annotation

    Architectural significance is annotated on the anchor of the unit that realizes it. A code anchor may carry role, the architectural pattern the unit plays; a component: anchor may additionally carry layer, one of edge, application, domain, adapter, or infrastructure, and context, its bounded context. The component: anchor is anchored architecture: it is the declared component, and there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized. It is not the original design's declared Component that could exist before code; an unrealized component lives in Specs and never as an invented CodeNode. A role is a free, corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts from the graph; service, decider, projection, read-model, codec, contract, barrel, and utility are the lineage set, not a closed list. layer is a closed set, and a value outside it is an envelope error; layer or context on a non-component anchor is an envelope error. All three attributes are optional, and omission is lawful.

Intent
outcome
Execute the watched-parameters rule on a parameter file, outside the probe root, that gains a key after the first cycle.
assumptions
  • The world writes the probe corpus of the error example, a parameter file outside the probe root holding { "one": 1 }, a first rules file whose body returns one warning finding for each key of its params, named by --rules and followed by --params @PATH naming that file, and the second rules file of the copy example. It starts the watcher as the rules-edit example does and, after the first cycle, writes { "one": 1, "two": 2 } to the parameter file, then reads the second cycle's corpus summary line and stops the watcher.
Behavior

Examples

Given a probe corpus the Protocol's validators find clean
Given a first rules file that {first: "reads a parameter file that gains a key after the first cycle under --watch"}
Given a second rules file that returns one warning when the graph it receives holds no node
When the probe corpus is validated with the rules files named by --rules in that order
Then the second cycle's corpus summary line reads {corpusSummary: "corpus rules: 0 errors · 2 warnings · 0 of 2 files failed (the corpus's own rules)"}

spec:consumers.validate-watch

Validation re-runs while an author edits carriers

specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
problem
An author editing a Spec re-runs sdp validate by hand after every save.
outcome
Let sdp validate --watch re-run the one validation path on every carrier change and stay alive after findings, as a loop for authoring and never a second validation path.
Behavior
rule line 19 · specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md:19
sdp validate --watch [root] installs its watcher first, then runs the same validate path sdp validate runs, from scratch, once at start and again after every carrier create, change, delete or rename under the root.
rule line 20 · specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md:20
A carrier ends in .sdp.md, .sdp.gherkin or .sdp.ts. The watcher ignores the directories discovery skips, the configured exclusion prefixes and every non-carrier path other than the rules files and parameter files --rules names, which it watches wherever they live, as spec:validation.corpus-rules#rule.watchReruns and spec:validation.corpus-rules#rule.watchedParams state; a removed watched directory and an event with no filename each schedule a run because their affected carriers cannot be named.
rule line 21 · specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md:21
Events that arrive while a run is in progress coalesce into one pending run.
rule.operatorStop line 22 · specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md:22
Findings print as sdp validate prints them and the process stays alive; operator SIGINT terminates the process with exit 0 even while a rules body is active, without waiting for it. No further rules file runs or output is written after the stop.

no example exercises it

rule line 23 · specs/consumers/validate-watch.sdp.md:23
For sdp validate, --watch cannot combine with --check-clean, and it re-runs on carrier edits and on edits to the files --rules names, and never on source edits, so an author re-runs validation after editing an anchor. This rule restricts no other verb's --watch, which its own Spec states.

10. Address resolution and dependency cycles stay executable graph recipes

spec:consumers.agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes

Address resolution and dependency cycles stay executable graph recipes

spec:consumers.agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipesUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 4 design entries · 3 pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

A dependency cycle is data about the authored dependencies. The readiness floor reads each dependency target's stated rung without walking a chain.

An adopter's gate checks both with copies of these bodies in its own rules file. Each recipe therefore answers with findings beside its rows, so the shipped file runs unchanged as a rules file and a gate keeps no copy. A finding is data: the corpus that names the file as a rules file chooses to fail on it, and the recipe still refuses nothing.

Intent
problem
An adopter that cites entry addresses outside its Specs resolves each one with its own grammar, and a Spec can rest on itself through a dependsOn chain no one has traced.
outcome
Resolve a list of entry addresses and report every dependsOn cycle with catalog recipes, so neither is rebuilt by hand.
Behavior
rule line 28 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:28
Address resolution reads params.addresses, falling back to the catalog sample when absent, and returns one row per input in input order, repeats included; each row carries address, resolves, id, section, key, value, file, line and reason. A resolving row carries the entry text or value and its recorded file and line, null when unlocated, with reason null. A miss keeps id, section and key when parsed, keeps value, file and line null, and gives reason malformed for an input that is no entry address, a bare Spec id included, or spec, section or entry for an absent Spec, section or key; malformed carries expected, the grammar in one line, and section or entry carries available, the keys that section holds sorted in code-unit order.
rule line 29 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:29
Address resolution follows the checked-mentions address grammar: a design or ui key resolves as an own key other than description, a question key resolves when an open question carries it, a rule key resolves through behavior.ruleKeys to its rule or flow text, and a term key resolves through model.termKeys to its term's definition; totals count inputs, resolving rows and each miss reason.
rule line 30 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:30
Dependency cycles take no parameter other than severity and read the whole graph. They report every set of two or more Specs in which each Spec reaches every other through declared dependsOn edges, and every Spec that declares dependsOn on itself and belongs to no such set. An edge whose target is not a Spec in the graph is ignored.
rule line 31 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:31
Each reported set lists its members sorted by id in code-unit order and one cycle through it as a closed path that starts and ends at its first member. The cycle is the shortest such path, found by a breadth-first walk from the first member over targets in code-unit order and restricted to the set; a Spec that depends only on itself reports the path of that Spec twice. Sets are ordered by their first member, and the totals count the sets, the self-dependent Specs, and the Specs in any set.
rule line 32 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:32
Both recipes report their answers and never refuse an authored dependency cycle.
rule.addressFindings line 33 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:33
Address resolution answers with findings beside its totals and rows: one finding for each row that does not resolve, in input order, the catalog sample's rows included, so the shipped file runs as a rules file over the addresses its --params names.

rule.cycleFindings line 34 · specs/consumers/agent-surface.address-and-cycle-recipes.sdp.md:34
Dependency cycles answers with findings beside its totals and cycles: one finding for each entry of cycles, in that order, naming the first member and the closed path through the set.

14. A corpus checks the register tokens its prose cites

spec:validation.external-registers

A corpus checks the register tokens its prose cites

spec:validation.external-registersUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 8 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/validation/external-registers.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

A corpus written against an earlier design cites that design's numbered things by token: its decisions, laws, scenarios, and the extensions the corpus itself adds. The first adopter keeps such a register as a table in its design README and checks the tokens its Specs cite against it with a script that reads the carriers a second way (libar-platform/design/tools/check.py). A register is the corpus's own data and never the Protocol's. A token stays prose: the carrier gains no grammar for it and the graph mints no node for it. Recipe 50 reads the tokens the Specs already hold as text, finds them by a pattern the corpus gives, checks them against a register file the corpus passes, and answers with findings, so the check runs as a rules file on the one validation path. Which registers a corpus may cite, and so which files it passes, is its owner's ruling.

Intent
problem
A corpus that cites the tokens of an outside register checks them with a script that reads its carriers a second way, or does not check them at all.
outcome
Check the tokens a corpus cites from an outside register against a register file it supplies, as a rules file, with no new grammar and no graph node.
Behavior
rule.tokensStayProse line 27 · specs/validation/external-registers.sdp.md:27
A register token stays prose: the carrier gains no grammar for it, the graph holds no node or edge for it, and no Protocol validator reads it.

no example exercises it

External registers, recipe 50, takes the register as data, a file the corpus passes with --params register=@PATH, and the pattern that finds the register's tokens in text, and reads the graph and nothing else.

no example exercises it

17. Every verb answers --help, and one verb writes every projection root

spec:consumers.command-line

Every verb answers --help, and one verb writes every projection root

spec:consumers.command-lineUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 5 design entries · 2 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

An adopter meets the command line one verb at a time, and the verb itself is the natural place to ask how it works. Each publisher's build first removes all five projection roots, so after one publisher runs only its own root is current, and writing all five took a script private to this repository. One public verb writes every root from one graph in one run, so an adopter's checkout and its CI publish the same set the Protocol's own does.

Intent
actor
An adopter, or an agent working for one, at the command line or in CI.
problem
A verb refuses --help instead of explaining itself, and no public verb publishes every projection root at once, so an adopter runs the publishers one by one and is left with only the last one's root.
outcome
Let every verb explain itself through --help, and let one verb write every projection root from one graph in one run.
Behavior
rule.verbHelp line 31 · specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md:31
Every verb answers --help: when --help is among a verb's arguments, the verb prints its help on standard output and exits 0, reading no other argument, deriving no graph and touching no file, a projection root included.

spec:consumers.command-line.verb-help-touches-nothing · enabled

rule.oneHelpText line 32 · specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md:32
A verb's help opens with its usage and its paragraph from the top-level help, the same text, so a verb's help and sdp --help never disagree; only the scaffolder's help, for sdp new and sdp new spec, adds a paragraph of its own after that text.

spec:consumers.command-line.verb-help-touches-nothing · enabled

sdp generate [root] [--exclude PATH]... [--vault DIR] [--check-clean] enters the shared build once, validates the graph, synchronizes the vault, and writes all five projection roots from that one graph: the Design Review, the census, the Mermaid diagrams, the Gherkin-shaped view and the Studio.

spec:consumers.command-line.generate-writes-every-root · enabled

rule.sameBytes line 34 · specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md:34
Each root the verb writes holds the bytes its own publisher writes from the same graph, written wholesale through its temporary sibling as that publisher writes it.

spec:consumers.command-line.generate-writes-every-root · enabled

rule.generateExit line 35 · specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md:35
Findings never withhold a root: the verb writes all five and exits with the validation exit code, and a graph that does not derive writes no root and exits 1.

spec:consumers.command-line.generate-writes-every-root · enabled

rule.generateCheck line 36 · specs/consumers/command-line.sdp.md:36
With --check-clean, the verb applies to each root the check its publisher applies under --check-clean, to renders of the one graph; a root that fails its check is removed, the others are written, and the run exits 1.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.shipped-projections-frozen

    Re-specifying the shipped Design Review, census, Mermaid, or Gherkin projection is refused. These four projections are the ruled read surfaces over the one graph. A later decision Spec that supersedes this one replaces the ruling whole; a decision Spec that refines this one narrows it for one projection or one rendering and leaves the rest frozen. Either passes the ADR three-part test.

specs/consumers/command-line.generate-check-failure.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Execute the check rule of the all-roots verb over five current roots, one of which holds a page its publisher would not write.
assumptions
  • The world writes the extraction root of the generate example, runs sdp generate on it so every root is current, since each publisher alone would leave only its own root, then plants one stale page in the census root. It runs sdp generate --check-clean on the root, then checks that the census root is gone and that each other root's files equal the files its own publisher writes when run alone on a copy of the same root. Lists of roots read as in the generate example.
Behavior

Examples

Given an extraction root holding two authored Specs and {roots: "five current projection roots, one stale page planted in the census root"}
When the command {command: "sdp generate --check-clean"} runs at that root
Then the command exits {exitCode: 1}
Then the stale pages survive: {staleSurvive: false}
Then the roots holding the current pages for those Specs are {currentRoots: "design-review, mermaid, gherkin, spec-studio"}
Then the absent projection roots are {absentRoots: "census"}

21. An example step may carry a key that survives rewording

spec:carrier.step-keys

An example step may carry a key that survives rewording

spec:carrier.step-keysBusiness Rule · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 9 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · 1 decision

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

A test that binds an example through bindExample names each step it handles, and an oracle names each Then step of its example space as an outcome kind. Both names are the step's skeleton, the step text with each slot reduced to its name, so rewording a step renames it and the typecheck fails at every handler and oracle that names it; a generated registrar holds its own handlers and changes with the contract when it is regenerated, so behind a registrar only the oracle's kinds hold a step's name. That break is the right default for a step whose words are its meaning, and the wrong one when an author improves the wording of a step that many examples and tests share. A step key separates the two. An author keys a step once, in the vocabulary its sibling examples share, and the key, not the wording, names the step in the contract and in the test. The key serves the build and the test, not prose: nothing outside an example and its test cites a single step, so the address grammar gains no step segment.

Intent
problem
A test that binds an example's steps directly names each by its text, and an oracle names each Then step the same way, so improving a step's wording breaks every test and oracle that names it, though nothing the step means has changed.
outcome
Let an example step carry a key in a marker, so its contract key and the binding a test holds survive a change of wording, in the Markdown, Gherkin and TypeScript carriers alike.
Rule

The world writes one extraction root holding a parent probe Spec and one child example in the carrier the slot names. The parent is a story-altitude behavior Spec stating scoped, with an Intent outcome, one rule and an example space whose Given steps are the steps the vocabulary slot joins with a semicolon and a space, followed by When the probe runs and Then the probe ends with {result:string}. The child is an example stating scoped that refines and verifies the parent, whose Given steps are the steps the example slot joins the same way, followed by When the probe runs and Then the probe ends with {result: "done"}. In Markdown the two are separate carriers; in Gherkin they are the Feature and one Scenario of one .sdp.gherkin file, with the vocabulary in its @example-space pseudo-scenario; in TypeScript they are two .sdp.ts carriers whose step strings are the same steps. The world extracts the root and generates the contracts, replaces every occurrence of the before text with the after text in every step as written, markers included, and extracts and generates again. A finding read is the first extraction finding of the first run, or the first contract-generation finding of the first run that names the child, and an empty slot value means the run reports none. A binding key is the key the child's step contract gives its first Given step, in the first run and then in the second, and an empty string when no step contract is emitted for the child. The world writes one bindExample handler map against the first contract, one handler per contract key, each declaring its parameters with the names and types that contract gives them and recording which handler each step reaches; it typechecks that unchanged map against the second contract and, when the typecheck passes, runs it with the second contract through planExample and runExamplePlan. stillBound is true only when the unchanged map typechecks and the reworded step reaches the handler it reached in the first run; a changed contract key, slot name or declared slot type makes it false. The import reads the carriers as reworded: the world imports each TypeScript carrier to Markdown, reads the emitted fence line of the parent's first Given step, extracts the imported carriers in a fresh root, and compares each Spec's step keys and step text with the TypeScript graph's.

rule.stepMarker line 23 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:23
A step may open its text with a step key marker, [#key] and one space, after its keyword: in a line of a gwt or gwt-vocabulary fence, in a step of a .sdp.gherkin Scenario or @example-space pseudo-scenario, and at the start of a step string in the TypeScript carrier. The key is lower-camel ASCII, the grammar every marker key follows, and an unkeyed step stays lawful. Importing a TypeScript carrier to Markdown writes the marker on every step that carries the key.

rule line 24 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:24
The marker is carrier syntax: the graph holds the step text without it and records the key apart, so the slot notation, the skeleton, the vocabulary match, the bound point, the readiness floor and the frozen projections read the step text unchanged.
rule.markerRefusals line 25 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:25
Step text that opens with [# and does not continue as a marker is refused at its step; a marker later in the text is plain text.

spec:carrier.step-keys.malformed-marker-refused · enabled

rule.oneKeyOneStep line 26 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:26
Within one Spec a key names one step and a step carries one key, a step being one skeleton: a key on two skeletons, or two keys on one skeleton, is refused at each step that carries one. A step written more than once needs its marker once and may repeat it. An example space belongs to one Spec, so its keys are unique across the space and the sibling set that binds it. A refused Markdown or Gherkin carrier is refused whole, as for every structure refusal; in the TypeScript carrier the key drops at each site and the Spec stays.

rule.vocabularyHome line 27 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:27
A sibling set shares its parent's vocabulary, and so its keys: an example step that resolves to a step of its parent's example space takes that step's key. A marker on such a step must repeat that key; any other marker, or a marker where the vocabulary step has none, withholds the example's step contract. An example step that no parent's example space declares takes its key from its own marker.

rule.contractKey line 28 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:28
A step's contract key is its key when it has one and its skeleton otherwise, as spec:extraction.executable-contracts derives it. The contract key names the step in the generated contract, the handler a test binds to it, and, for a Then step of an example space, the kind of its outcome.

rule line 29 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:29
A key names the step and its slots name the step's parameters: the handler bound under a key receives the step's bound values, typed by the vocabulary as an unkeyed handler's are, and a key never names a slot.
rule.rewordedStaysBound line 30 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:30
Rewording a keyed step, in the vocabulary and in every example that uses it, leaves its contract key unchanged, so a directly authored handler bound under the key, and an oracle that names it as an outcome kind, compile and run unchanged; an adopted registrar is regenerated, as after every carrier edit, and its authored adapters compile unchanged. Renaming or retyping one of its slots changes its parameters and breaks the binding, as it always has.

spec:carrier.step-keys.gherkin-keyed-step-stays-bound · enabled, spec:carrier.step-keys.reworded-keyed-step-stays-bound · enabled

rule.unkeyedBreaks line 31 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:31
An unkeyed step is keyed by its skeleton, as it always was: rewording it changes its contract key. A directly authored handler under the old skeleton fails the typecheck as a missing and an excess property and fails the run at that step; a committed adopted registrar fails the regeneration preflight until it is regenerated; and an oracle that names a reworded Then step by its old kind fails the typecheck.

spec:carrier.step-keys.reworded-unkeyed-step-breaks · enabled

rule.renamedKey line 32 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:32
Renaming or removing a key changes the step's contract key: a directly authored handler under the old key fails the typecheck, and when the key names a Then step of the example space, an oracle that names its old outcome kind fails the typecheck too. A key changes only when an author changes it.

spec:carrier.step-keys.renamed-key-breaks · enabled

rule line 33 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:33
A step key is not an entry address: the address grammar gains no step segment, prose cites no step, and the location table records none. The generated contract and the code bound to it are a key's only readers, and the typechecker holds them to it; a review that cites one step cites its example Spec and the rules that example exercises.
rule line 34 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:34
A step key mints no edge, confers no delivery fact and moves no readiness floor.

stepMarker line 51 · specs/carrier/step-keys.sdp.md:51
<keyword> [#<key>] <text> is a keyed step in a gwt or gwt-vocabulary fence line and in a .sdp.gherkin step, with <keyword> one of Given, When, Then and And, and "[#<key>] <text>" is a keyed TypeScript step string; <key> matches ^[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]*$.

behavior.stepKeys maps each key to the skeleton of the step it names, in authored order, the example space's steps before the examples' steps; the step strings hold the text with the marker removed; a Spec with no keyed step carries no stepKeys, and the serialized graph writes it after exampleSpace.

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.shipped-projections-frozen

    Re-specifying the shipped Design Review, census, Mermaid, or Gherkin projection is refused. These four projections are the ruled read surfaces over the one graph. A later decision Spec that supersedes this one replaces the ruling whole; a decision Spec that refines this one narrows it for one projection or one rendering and leaves the rest frozen. Either passes the ADR three-part test.

Intent
outcome

Examples

Then the first extraction finding's message contains {extractMessage: ""}

specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Give bound tests typed step contracts and space contracts without reading authored Specs directly.
Behavior
rule line 22 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:22
generateContracts derives per-example step contracts and per-parent space contracts solely from the extracted graph.
rule line 23 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:23
A generated contract is disposable, keyed by Spec ID, and withheld when its example is not in the bindable form or its steps do not resolve against the shared vocabulary.
rule.concreteness line 24 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:24
The concreteness law is a refusal, never a guess — an example carrying an unbound slot in any used step of any entry is not the bindable form and receives no step contract, and a prose-only example receives none either.

spec:extraction.executable-contracts.concreteness-refusal · enabled

rule line 25 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:25
Concreteness reads the example's own form, whether or not a parent declares shared vocabulary. Vocabulary resolution is a separate later check; incompatible resolution withholds the step contract with contracts/unmatched-vocabulary-step.
rule.onePoint line 26 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:26
An example is one point, so the step contract and bound point derive from the same first complete structured Given/When/Then entry. A further entry, which the TypeScript carrier can carry, is named contracts/multi-entry-example rather than left silently inert.

spec:extraction.executable-contracts.multi-entry-example · enabled

rule.contractKeys line 27 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:27
Each step of a step contract carries its contract key beside its skeleton: its step key, from its own marker or from the vocabulary step it resolves to, under spec:carrier.step-keys, and its skeleton when it has none. The Step union and the StepParams properties are the contract keys in first-occurrence order, and the runner dispatches each step to the handler bound under its contract key.

spec:carrier.step-keys.reworded-keyed-step-stays-bound · enabled, spec:carrier.step-keys.reworded-unkeyed-step-breaks · enabled

rule line 28 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:28
Degradation is loud and local: an undeclared slot or a value outside its declared type is named and left out of the bound point; an off-type value stays in the step contract, widened to its scalar kind, so the emitted module still compiles; and a conflicting re-binding is named and its first value wins, in the bound point for a slot bound twice and in the step contract for a step that recurs with other values.
rule line 29 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:29
A vocabulary slot group that declares no usable type is named rather than dropped in silence, and no dimension enters the space for it.
rule.outcomeIdentity line 30 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:30
Each Then step of the parent's example space is one variant of the space contract's Outcome union, whose kind is that step's contract key, its step key or else its skeleton text; the build derives no slug or ordinal, and the runner core adds unspecified.

no example exercises it

rule.keyConflicts line 31 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:31
A contract never holds two steps under one contract key. An example marker that disagrees with the key of its vocabulary step withholds the example's step contract with contracts/conflicting-step-key. A step or space contract whose steps would share a contract key, two skeletons under one key or a key equal to another step's skeleton, is withheld with contracts/duplicate-step-key, naming the key and both skeletons; a withheld space contract withholds every registrar of its children.

spec:carrier.step-keys.conflicting-example-key-withheld · enabled, spec:carrier.step-keys.key-equal-to-a-skeleton-withheld · enabled

rule.caseCollision line 32 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:32
Two contract paths differing only by letter case cannot coexist on a case-insensitive filesystem, so the contracts tree is withheld whole and the finding names the colliding pair.

spec:extraction.executable-contracts.case-colliding-path · enabled

rule line 33 · specs/extraction/executable-contracts.sdp.md:33
Every generation finding is a warning that describes what did not emit; gating belongs to graph validation alone, so a withheld contract never fails the build by itself.

33. Derived runnable modules freeze the registrar interface

spec:extraction.runnable-modules

Derived runnable modules freeze the registrar interface

spec:extraction.runnable-modulesUse Case / Behavior · featureready floor ready

specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
problem
A bound example test would otherwise repeat registration, step dispatch and oracle comparison that the graph and contracts already determine.
outcome
Give each bindable example a generated registrar, so its authored test keeps semantics derivation cannot supply.
value
A Spec and a small authored semantics module express the test while the engine neither loads nor executes adopter code.
Behavior
rule line 28 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:28
Code generation emits a registrar called with createWorld, invoke, observe, expected and optional assertions. It owns describe/it registration, step dispatch, the three-way comparator and failure rendering. The authored test keeps its top-level specTest anchor and one activation call beside its semantics. The authored file imports the generated registrar; the generated module imports no authored code. Normal runner discovery loads the authored file and activates registration. Generated modules never self-register; the graph records binding, never liveness.
rule line 29 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:29
Generated sibling path — for each bindable example, codegen emits exactly one generated registration module as a sibling *.generated.ts of the authored .test.ts (deterministic filename keyed by Spec ID, not by the authored suite filename). One authored suite may verify many examples without their registrar map keys or output paths colliding. Exactly one generated registration per example; a second registration path for the same example is refused. Generated siblings are disposable build output: an adopted registrar is committed because authored code imports it, while unadopted registrars remain ignored, regenerable output and confer no migration claim.
rule line 30 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:30
generated/registrars.json is a versioned, sorted manifest of every extraction-root-relative registrar sibling owed by the build. Publication reconciles the manifest and removes siblings no longer owed under the build-pipeline law. --check-clean compares the manifest and every sibling byte with fresh generation. Preflight independently compares every tracked adopted registrar in the worktree and Git index with regenerated bytes.
rule line 31 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:31
Registration-path loudness — multiple anchors in one authored suite still locate one registrar sibling; when one example resolves to more than one distinct authored suite path, generation emits a named finding and withholds that registrar rather than selecting a path silently.
rule line 32 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:32
Generated registrars import shared runtime helpers from @libar-dev/software-delivery-protocol/testing and types through public package subpaths. Public exports are the root for model, anchors and public types, ./anchors for zero-dependency anchor builders, ./runner for the framework-neutral plan/run core, ./vitest for bindExample, and ./testing for the registrar runtime. Authored suites may import anchor builders through the root or ./anchors. Authored and generated modules never import private src paths. The supported optional Vitest peer range is >=2, as declared by the package.
rule line 33 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:33
Step identity is the step's contract key: its step key under spec:carrier.step-keys, or its skeleton text when it has none, and generation introduces no ordinal or slug identity. A directly authored bindExample handler map fails the typecheck when one of its keys goes stale. An adopted registrar holds no authored per-step handler: a stale committed registrar fails the regeneration preflight, and its internal handlers change with the contract when it is regenerated. The contract key of a Then step of the example space also names an Outcome kind, so changing it fails the typecheck of an authored oracle that names the old kind.
rule line 34 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:34
Handler resolution — the generated registrar's internal dispatch object is an exhaustive mapped type over the contract's step keys: removing or staling one of those generated callbacks is a tsc error naming that step. The adopted authored surface retains no per-step callbacks (and therefore no step keys); its five adapters are required keys (assertions optional), so a missing or stale authored callback is a tsc error naming that adapter. These are the two exhaustive mapped-type checks; demanding an authored error name a step while simultaneously retaining no authored per-step surface is refused as contradictory. Codegen cannot statically see authored handlers, so no generation-time handler refusal is promised — the type system carries it. Existing generation-time refusals (unbindable example, incompatible vocabulary, colliding path) are reused unchanged.
rule line 35 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:35
Scenario-level invocation — the five-adapter interface carries one product invoke per example, so the first When occurrence invokes it and later When occurrences in the same lawful scenario do not repeat side effects.
rule line 36 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:36
At the first Then, the comparator refuses an incomplete point before calling the oracle and otherwise evaluates and caches expected(point). It finds the authored Then whose contract key equals expected.kind, compares that step's authored parameters with the oracle payload, reads observe(world), compares observed and oracle outcomes, and runs additional assertions separately. Actual-equals-oracle alone is insufficient: a Spec parameter mutation must fail. The oracle accepts Partial<Conditions>; the registrar never casts a partial point to Conditions.
rule line 37 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:37
Oracle payload versus Spec Then parameters and observed versus oracle outcomes use deep structural equality on the authored shape. Diagnostics name missing, extra or changed values by path and show expected and actual values. The comparator quotes authored Then parameters and skeleton text without rephrasing them.
rule line 38 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:38
Failure rendering reuses the contract's matching Then step plus the existing renderContractStep path. When the oracle selected no authored Then, emit a scenario-level diagnostic quoting Spec ID, oracle kind, and the contract keys of the available Then steps; preserve the original assertion as cause.
rule line 39 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:39
Bound unspecified outcome — unspecified names a coverage gap in the example space, but a bound executable example selecting it reddens because no authored Then may silently witness that gap.
rule line 40 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:40
The authored top-level specTest carries a non-empty verifies target naming the example. It remains the source of has-verifier; generated execution confers no delivery fact and records no pass state.
rule line 41 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:41
Additive assertions — optional assertions may add domain checks the Outcome union cannot express; they never replace steps (3) or (5) of the three-way comparator and never silence a Spec-param or oracle mismatch.
rule line 42 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:42
Case mapping and outlines — outline rows map one deterministic case per row in carrier order when a multi-row table sugar expands statically into sibling examples (point-per-example). Scenario Outlines and inline Examples tables stay refused as executable carrier constructs inside a single example; one example remains one point and earns exactly one generated registration.
rule line 43 · specs/extraction/runnable-modules.sdp.md:43
Registrars use no environment, global or module side channel, mutable global registry or singleton world shared across examples. Generated siblings export the registrar and never self-register. Generation derives no domain observation; the engine never loads or executes adopter code. Registrars do not become generated test harnesses. Scenario Outlines stay refused. The interface changes neither the claim taxonomy, anchor bindings nor the contract-key identity of steps.

Requirement drawing

Decisions

  • spec:decisions.adopted-registrars-committed

    A registrar becomes adopted when tracked authored code imports it. Adopted registrars are committed and byte-checked against fresh generation; unadopted registrars remain ignored, regenerable output. A deterministic generated manifest owns reconciliation for both groups without turning registrar content into authored truth.

  • spec:decisions.anchor-comment-form

    An anchor has two extracted representations that feed one closed envelope, the constant form as ruled and a comment form. The comment form is a top-level /** … */ block in a .ts or .tsx file carrying reserved camelCase, TSDoc-compatible tags; @sdpAnchor <id> opens it, and the id's namespace selects the flavor exactly as the constant builders do. Comment prose still authors nothing: only the reserved tags are read, and a comment that does not open with /** is never read. Trust is by reserved grammar, not by builder import, so no import is required. The same id in two forms is a duplicate id. The package also ships a zero-dependency subpath @libar-dev/software-delivery-protocol/anchors exporting the id builders and the three anchor builders and nothing else, for runtimes that may import but must not load node:* modules or ts-morph; the extractor trusts that specifier as a Protocol builder module.

  • spec:decisions.binding-not-liveness

    Delivery facts record bindings and enabled verifier existence; coverage gaps and human readiness practice remain explicit without becoming graph facts.

  • spec:decisions.point-per-example

    An example binds exactly one point; table syntax may expand statically into sibling examples and renderers may project siblings as a table.

34. A Model term may carry a key that addresses it

spec:model.term-addresses

A Model term may carry a key that addresses it

spec:model.term-addressesBusiness Rule · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:obsidian-vault-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 10 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · 2 decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle none.

A Model section defines a Spec's terms, and prose names those terms by word. A word is not a checked entry address, so a view cannot resolve it to one authored definition, and a renamed term leaves every sentence that names it silently stale. Design, UI, question and rule entries already carry keys that a mention addresses and validation checks; a key gives a Model term the same. The key is authored in a marker, as a rule's is, rather than derived from the term: a derived key would change, and break every address, whenever the term is reworded. The address segment is term, because an address names the kind of entry it reaches, as question and rule do, and the Model section's own prose is not an entry. The ratified glossary stays a document, beside the graph and outside it, so its terms gain no address; a term gains one where a Spec defines it.

Intent
problem
Prose that names a concept a Model section defines has no checked way to point at that definition, so a view cannot link it and a renamed term breaks its readers silently.
outcome
Let a Model term carry a key, addressed as spec:<id>#term.<key>, so prose cites a concept as a checked mention and every view links it exactly.
Rule

The world writes two carriers in one extraction root. The first is a story-altitude model Spec stating scoped, with an Intent outcome and a Model section holding the entries the terms slot joins with a semicolon and a space, in the carrier the slot names: in Markdown one line each, as written, and in TypeScript a .sdp.ts carrier whose model.terms object maps each entry's term to its definition, marker included. The second is a Markdown story-altitude rule Spec stating idea, with an Intent outcome and one rule; its narrative names the address, and it declares dependsOn on the first. A finding read is the first extraction finding, and an empty slot value means the extraction reports none; the term keys of every Spec in the graph are joined by a comma and a space. resolved is true when address resolution gives the address a resolving row whose value is the definition without its marker and whose file and line are those of the term's row in the location table. found is true when entry search for the words of the term that carries the address's key returns a row with that address and that line. The audit reason is the reason of the mention audit's unresolved row for the address, and empty when it lists none. The import reads the first carrier as written in TypeScript: the world imports it to Markdown, reads the emitted Model entry of its first term, extracts the imported carrier in a fresh root, and compares its term keys and definitions with the TypeScript graph's.

rule.termMarker line 32 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:32
A Model term may carry an optional key in a marker that opens its definition, after the bold term and the em dash, as in - **step key** — [#stepKey] the key a step carries; the TypeScript carrier writes the same marker at the start of the definition string. The key follows the entry-address key grammar, and an unkeyed term stays lawful and has no address. Importing a TypeScript carrier to Markdown writes the marker on the term that carries the key.

termMarker line 60 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:60
- **<term>** — [#<key>] <definition> is a keyed Model entry in Markdown and terms: { "<term>": "[#<key>] <definition>" } in TypeScript; <key> matches ^[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]*$, and a marker later in the definition is plain text.

no citation recorded

termKeysField line 61 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:61
model.termKeys maps each key to the term it names, as authored, in authored order; the definitions hold the text with the marker removed; a Spec with no keyed term carries no termKeys, and the serialized graph writes it after terms.

no citation recorded

markerRefusal line 62 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:62
term key markers must be [#<lower-camel ASCII key>] followed by one space and text is the message, as the finding extract/unrecognized-property at severity error, at path model.terms.<term>.

no citation recorded

repeatedKey line 63 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:63
term key "<key>" is repeated; term keys must be unique within a Spec is the message, as the same finding, at each term that carries the key.

no citation recorded

addressSections line 64 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:64
ENTRY_ADDRESS_SECTIONS is ["design", "ui", "question", "rule", "term"], and parseId refuses any other segment with entry address must be <section>.<key> with section design, ui, question, rule, or term.

no citation recorded

missingTerm line 65 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:65

no citation recorded

termLocation line 66 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:66
{ spec, file, entry: "term[<i>]", key?, line } is a term's row in the location table; a mention in a definition, at model.terms.<term>, takes that row's line.

no citation recorded

resolutionRow line 67 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:67
address resolution (recipe 25) reads term through model.termKeys; a resolving row gives the marker-free definition as value and its recorded file and line. A section or entry miss gives the available term keys sorted in code-unit order. The grammar text is spec:<id>#<section>.<key>, section design, ui, question, rule, or term; key lower-camel ASCII.
searchRow line 68 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:68
entry search (recipe 23) gives a matching keyed term, in section model and entry terms.<term>, the address spec:<id>#term.<key> and the line of its term[<i>] row, matches the term key as it matches a rule key, and never walks termKeys as content.
importEmitter line 69 · specs/model/term-addresses.sdp.md:69
the TypeScript-to-Markdown import writes a keyed term as - **<term>** — [#<key>] <definition>, so a keyed TypeScript term imports keyed.

Design view

Requirement drawing

  • Declared verifying examples: no declared verifying example.

Decisions

  • A Spec id written in prose is a checked mention

    A Spec id in narrative or section text, outside gwt and gwt-vocabulary fences, is a mention. A mention that does not resolve is a conformance error. A mention of another Spec that shares no declared relation with the mentioning Spec, in either direction, is one warning per mentioning Spec and target Spec pair, whatever the number of locations; an address on the mentioning Spec's own id is checked for its entry and never warned. An entry address is a Spec id followed by #, the section name design, ui, question, rule, or term, a dot, and the entry's lower-camel ASCII key, as in spec:<id>#design.<key> or spec:<id>#question.<key>. A design or ui address resolves when the Spec exists and that section holds the key as its own key, other than description; a question address resolves when the Spec exists and one of its open questions carries that key; a term address resolves when the Spec exists and one of its Model terms carries that key. The # sub-part is reserved for the entry address in every namespace: a Spec's own id, a relation target, a Pack member or model reference, an anchor id or target, and the specId and ref builders all refuse it. A mention mints no edge, and the reader gains no join.

  • spec:decisions.shipped-projections-frozen

    Re-specifying the shipped Design Review, census, Mermaid, or Gherkin projection is refused. These four projections are the ruled read surfaces over the one graph. A later decision Spec that supersedes this one replaces the ruling whole; a decision Spec that refines this one narrows it for one projection or one rendering and leaves the rest frozen. Either passes the ADR three-part test.

40. A Spec id written in prose is a checked mention

spec:decisions.checked-mentions

A Spec id written in prose is a checked mention

spec:decisions.checked-mentionsDecision Record · featureready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: no design entries · no pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/decisions/checked-mentions.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding none, verifier binding none, and expected-outcome oracle none.

Intent
outcome
Make a Spec id written in prose resolve, and make one keyed entry of an open section, one keyed open question, one keyed entry of the primary behavior owner, or one keyed Model term addressable, so a reference below the Spec level can be checked.
Decision
context
Specs name other Specs, and single entries of them, in prose. Referential integrity reads edges and Pack references only. A prose id that does not resolve passes validation, a mention that no relation backs hides a dependent from blast radius, and finding every Spec that repeats an entry is a text search. The first adopter corpus carried its design as keyed entries, and most of its prose mentions had no declared relation.
decision
A Spec id in narrative or section text, outside gwt and gwt-vocabulary fences, is a mention. A mention that does not resolve is a conformance error. A mention of another Spec that shares no declared relation with the mentioning Spec, in either direction, is one warning per mentioning Spec and target Spec pair, whatever the number of locations; an address on the mentioning Spec's own id is checked for its entry and never warned. An entry address is a Spec id followed by #, the section name design, ui, question, rule, or term, a dot, and the entry's lower-camel ASCII key, as in spec:<id>#design.<key> or spec:<id>#question.<key>. A design or ui address resolves when the Spec exists and that section holds the key as its own key, other than description; a question address resolves when the Spec exists and one of its open questions carries that key; a term address resolves when the Spec exists and one of its Model terms carries that key. The # sub-part is reserved for the entry address in every namespace: a Spec's own id, a relation target, a Pack member or model reference, an anchor id or target, and the specId and ref builders all refuse it. A mention mints no edge, and the reader gains no join.
rationale
  • The warning asks for a relation that already exists, so linkage keeps one home. A relation in either direction backs a mention because blast radius walks its one hop both ways, so a reverse edge already surfaces the dependent. One warning per pair keeps the report readable where a Spec names one neighbor in many bullets, and the mention audit keeps every location.
  • This applies the content-only sections ruling rather than contradicting it. A mention mints no edge, so no consumer branches on a reference union, and the warning names the double-linkage drift the earlier ruling left legal and silent. The id grammar already parses and formats a # sub-part; this record gives it its only meaning, and the dot inside the sub-part is the one grammar change.
  • The owner ruled that an open question may carry an optional key in its marker, as in - [blocking #aggregateReach] text, addressed as spec:<id>#question.aggregateReach. The key grammar is the Design key grammar, a key is unique among one Spec's open questions, and an unkeyed question stays lawful. A register that cites a question by its position breaks silently when a question above it moves or closes, and the first adopter's register had drifted in such citations; a key breaks loudly where it is renamed.
  • The owner ruled that the address carries the section, because open-section keys are unique within a section and not within a Spec, so spec:<id>#design.shared and spec:<id>#ui.shared stay distinct when one carrier holds both; that # is refused in every identity, because neither this corpus nor the first adopter's carries one, and one meaning per sub-part keeps resolution a lookup instead of a precedence rule; and that one lower-camel key grammar serves every carrier, so an address is typeable from memory and a lawful TypeScript key outside it is simply unaddressable.
  • A Model term carries an authored key in a marker that opens its definition, as a rule carries its own, addressed through the segment term. A key derived from the term would break every address whenever the term is reworded, and the segment names the kind of entry, as question and rule do. The ratified glossary stays a document, so its terms gain no address; a term gains one where a Spec defines it.
alternatives
  • A new edge type for mentions costs the schema, the edge contract, the census, the Mermaid view, and every recipe that filters edges. The warning reaches the same dependents through relations that exist.
  • Leaving the check to each adopter's own lint fixes one corpus and no other.
  • A positional address for an unkeyed bullet, such as the third flow of a Workflow, was refused. Positions move with every edit above them, so such an address would break silently where a key breaks loudly.
  • Refusing a key that appears under both Design and UI would shorten the address and make one section's keys depend on the other's. Refused by the owner.
  • Letting an identity with # outrank an address would retain the earlier identity grammar and make every address resolution a two-step lookup for a case no corpus has. Refused by the owner.
  • Warning only on a missing forward relation would turn a parent's mention of its own child into a finding the child's refines edge already answers. Refused by the owner.
consequences
  • Keyed Design and UI entries, keyed open questions, keyed entries of the primary behavior owner and keyed Model terms are addressable, a rule address resolving when the Spec's behavior.ruleKeys carries the key and a term address when its model.termKeys does. Unkeyed entries have no address; a reference to one stays a Spec-level mention, and a sequence that must be addressed is authored as keyed entries.
  • The key description names the leading prose of a design or ui section and is never an entry there, so a design or ui address ending in .description never resolves. A question key is a value on the question, not a property beside section prose, so description is an ordinary question key. A TypeScript key outside the lower-camel ASCII grammar is lawful and has no address.
  • A renamed or removed open-section key, question key, rule key or term key fails validation in every Spec that addresses it.
  • Blast radius and delta review scope include a mentioning Spec once a declared relation backs its mention.
  • A family pattern written in id form reads as an unresolved mention, so such a pattern is written as plain words.
  • No reference check detects two Specs that restate one shape in their own words. The check narrows that defect class and never closes it.

41. The graph records where anchored source cites an entry address

spec:extraction.entry-citations

The graph records where anchored source cites an entry address

spec:extraction.entry-citationsUse Case / Behavior · storyready floor ready

Packs: pack:adopter-speed-v1, pack:self-hosting-v1

Design: 8 design entries · 7 pinned declarations · no decisions

Findings: no errors, no warnings

specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md

No open questions and no blocking questions; implementation binding present, verifier binding present, and expected-outcome oracle present.

A test that checks a pinned declaration names the entry in its own text, often as the test's title, and the graph does not see that link: a reader of the declaration finds the suite's file through its anchor but not the assertion. The first adopter's type test names each comparison by the address of the Design entry it binds (libar-platform/tests/types/pinned.test-d.ts), and a reader of its pages could not find the comparison for one declaration. The extractor already reads every anchored source file for its anchors, so it records where such a file writes an entry address, and a page or a recipe shows the line that checks a declaration.

A citation is where text names an entry, read by the machine from comments and strings. It carries the inferred claim and confers nothing, and it sits in a table beside the location table, as a position does. A citation is inferred location data in the graph. It adds no node or edge, confers no delivery fact, moves no readiness floor, feeds no Protocol validator and records no test verdict.

Intent
problem
A test that checks one pinned declaration names its entry address only in its own text, so no view links the declaration to the line that checks it, and a reader holding the declaration cannot find its assertion.
outcome
Record each entry address an anchored source file cites, with its file and line, as an inferred citation that confers nothing, so a view can show the test line that checks a pinned declaration.
Behavior
rule.anchoredFilesOnly line 30 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:30
The extractor reads citations from each source file it reads for anchors that carries at least one anchor, of either form and any namespace, after the same exclusions; a file that carries no anchor, a carrier and any other file is not read for citations.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.code-comment-cites-declaration · enabled, spec:extraction.entry-citations.test-title-cites-declaration · enabled, spec:extraction.entry-citations.unanchored-file-unread · enabled

rule.citationToken line 31 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:31
A citation is a token the prose-mention scan would read as a mention, found anywhere in such a file's text, in a comment, a string or a template literal, that holds #; a token followed by ${, directly or after the trailing punctuation the mention scan strips, is the prefix of a computed address and records no citation, whether or not the prefix parses as an entry address; a bare Spec id is not a citation.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.test-title-cites-declaration · enabled

rule.citationRow line 32 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:32
Each citation records the address as written, the file's root-relative path and the 1-based line the token starts on; one address written twice on one line is one row.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.test-title-cites-declaration · enabled

rule.citationTable line 33 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:33
The citations ride in a table of their own beside the location table, sorted and deterministic as the graph is, and Primitive and Pack nodes stay free of them.

no example exercises it

rule.inferredClaim line 34 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:34
The table's definition gives every citation the inferred claim, and every reader row of a citation carries it, so no consumer reads a citation as an authored binding.

no example exercises it

rule.confersNothing line 35 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:35
A citation mints no node or edge, confers no delivery fact, moves no readiness floor, feeds no Protocol validator and records no verdict on the citing file; removing every citation changes no node, edge, fact, floor or finding.

no example exercises it

rule.readerRows line 36 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:36
The reader resolves each citation by the rules address resolution applies, and the Spec context carries the citations whose address names that Spec as its entry citations, each with the entry it names, whether it resolves and why not, the citing file and line, the anchors recorded at that file and those of them that are test anchors verifying the Spec.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.test-title-cites-declaration · enabled, spec:extraction.entry-citations.unresolved-citation · enabled

rule.declarationLines line 37 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:37
Those rows let a view show, beside each pinned declaration of a Spec, the anchored lines that cite it, with no join of its own; a row reads as a test line only when a test: anchor at its file verifies the cited Spec, directly or through an example that verifies it, every other row stays a citation with its file and line, and no row says what a test asserts or whether it passed.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.code-comment-cites-declaration · enabled, spec:extraction.entry-citations.test-title-cites-declaration · enabled

rule.citationRecipe line 38 · specs/extraction/entry-citations.sdp.md:38
Entry citations, recipe 51, lists for a Pack, a list of Specs or the corpus each pinned declaration and every other cited entry with the lines that cite it, and every citation that does not resolve, and answers each citation that does not resolve, and only those, as a finding, so a corpus may name the shipped file as a rules file.

spec:extraction.entry-citations.unresolved-citation · enabled

An unresolved citation stays in the table and reports only through the reader's rows and the recipe's answer, never as a Protocol finding: whether it fails a gate is the corpus's choice of rules file.
